title: Agent Harness generic field manual (seed)
summary: Field rules of the cold-start seed template: credential discipline, subagent dispatch, evidence first, output conventions, harness mechanics. After copying this Mod a new project only edits its own project chapters and config; these five chapters can be reused as they are, and the play guide lives in the consumer's root document.

source.note: This resource is a **seed template**, not the rule projection of one repository: the five chapters are all generic meta-workflow discipline and contain no repository-specific directory structure, ports, remote URLs, deployment channels or gate commands. After copying this Mod the consumer writes its own project chapters in its own Mod (repository shape / branches and lanes / integration and deployment / gate commands / pointers / hard constraints); the two are fetched by section id and never overwrite each other. The evolution chapter (added 2026-11-01) is generic meta-workflow discipline: how to screen and review end-of-run evolution candidates. The harness chapter describes the harness mechanism itself (the two-layer state machine / action protocol / async entry / settlement / the Mod-change trio / the host contract) — it says how to use this harness, not how this repository legislates.

sections.title: 1. Credential discipline
sections.summary: Highest priority, non-negotiable: credentials never enter the repository, a conversation artifact or any committed surface; only key names appear, and every example is synthetic.

rules.text: Never write a credential, key or token into the repository — including code, documentation, commit messages and Mod example data.
Never write a credential into any conversation artifact: reports, summaries, issue/PR descriptions, pasted log excerpts.

No sensitive information may enter a committed resource — the committed surface explicitly includes: static configuration, the `data/playbook.json` rule resource, the experience/growth (evolution) Mod and its output, and every other Mod resource or document committed with the repository.
The runtime KV family `settings.*` is no exception for sensitive values: the static defaults and the dynamic overrides only ever hold non-sensitive behavior switches, numbers and explanatory text.
rules.basis: seed-template baseline (two-layer config: dynamic override > static default)

rules.text: Local credentials always go through `.env` / `.env.local` (both git-ignored, mode 600); `.env.example` carries key names only, never values.
Reports, documentation, commit messages, Mod resources and narrative text show key names only, never values — including the closing review and any walk report.
When auditing the environment-variable surface, read key names plus lengths only; never spread the raw output open or feed it into a tool that persists it.
rules.basis: seed-template baseline (handling discipline after a credential leak)

rules.text: Examples and test data are always synthetic; never introduce real personal data or real business metrics.

After a violation, list honestly what was exposed (the specific file, the content location and the actual returned content), without downplaying or arguing; then stop the affected operations and wait for the user.

sections.title: 2. Subagent dispatch discipline
sections.summary: Background dispatch never blocks the main session; dispatch parameters come from local env and are used for dispatch only; one workspace carries one task at a time; the executor never closes a run.

rules.text: After dispatching you must register the executor (a **self-declared ledger**, not identity proof): `config.set executor.<rN>.<stage>=<agent_id>`, stage ∈ analysis / plan / development; when one subagent covers all three stages, register the same id stage by stage. Replacing the executor for the same (req, stage) with a different id **requires** a reason (`=<new_id>|<reason>`); a **cross-stage handoff** (a plan id different from the analysis one, or — with no plan — different from the analysis one) equally requires a reason and may never be silently overwritten as a "first binding for that stage". A successful handoff writes `id|reason` and appends one entry to `req.<i>.hist` (reusing the rolling cap; no separate history/handoff key); a clean first binding writes no history. The ledger carries no rev: `amend` does not change the binding and `split` / `merge` do not inherit it. `proposal.submit` performs no hard check — an unregistered executor only shows as "unregistered" in `requirement.list` and never blocks external proposals or same-ext replays.
rules.basis: user decision 2026-11-01 (E2 ruling: reuse config.set, bind no rev, no hard submit gate, a cross-stage handoff must give a reason)

rules.text: Every subagent task runs in the background; the main session never waits in place — keep advancing other lanes, verifications or planning while it runs, and verify and merge once the completion notice arrives.
Synchronous waiting is allowed only when the next action strictly depends on the result and nothing else can progress in parallel; even then, spend the waiting time on other lanes first.

Dispatch parameters come from local `.env` / `.env.local` (such as `YGG_SUBAGENT_MODEL` / `YGG_SUBAGENT_THINKING`) and are used for dispatch options only; when unset, pass nothing explicitly and use the harness default.
Such parameter values are never printed, written into documentation, committed, or put into any report.
rules.basis: seed-template baseline (the dispatch surface of credential discipline)

rules.text: Require the target workspace to be clean before dispatching (local markers such as the plaque file excepted); settle a dirty tree first, otherwise the executor cannot tell which changes are its own.
One workspace carries exactly one task at any moment (lane serialization); different workspaces may run in parallel. Always check whether the workspace is already occupied before dispatching.

The executor (subagent) only implements its own stage and delivers after self-check; integration, merging and deployment are always executed serially by the main agent and never delegated to an executor.

sections.title: 3. Evidence first
sections.summary: A conclusion may come only from command output and its exit code, from an artifact file, or from the source text you actually read; when unsure, say you are unsure.

rules.text: Prove a point with command output and its exit code; when pasting a conclusion, give the actual command and its exit code in the same block.
Prove a point with an artifact's existence and content (existence plus the key content, not merely "it was generated").
When quoting source code, give `file:line`, never "I remember it somewhere".
Never assert from impression; never write evidence-free completion phrases such as "I have finished".
When unsure, say you are unsure and state how it will be verified next.
A check that is not wired up must be declared "not covered" in the report; it never passes by default or is left unmentioned.

sections.title: 4. Language and output
sections.summary: Chinese conversation, English identifiers; conclusion before evidence; read before editing; print a mechanical rewrite before writing it and read it back afterwards.

rules.text: Talk to the user in Chinese; keep code, identifiers, paths and commands in their original English.
For an error or a conclusion, state the conclusion first and the evidence after it.
Read a file before editing it; when editing several files, explain file by file what changed and why.
For a large mechanical rewrite (especially Markdown tree structures and tables) print the result first, then write it, then immediately read it back to verify.

sections.title: 5. Agent Harness mechanics
sections.summary: Two-layer state machine + two mandatory gates + action protocol + async entry + settlement criteria + the Mod-change trio + the host contract: this chapter only says how the machine turns; a project's own rules go in its own chapters.

rules.text: goal authorization is a **run-level self-declared record**: `config.set goal.authorization=<one-line note>` writes `settings.goal.authorization` (trimmed, ≤ 200 characters, no newline; an empty value clears it explicitly). Only runs that entered goal **at runtime** (`settings.play.mode=goal`) are checked before `review.note` closes: a missing record blocks with a narrative line, writes no `ending` and does not advance; a static `goal` preset in `data/config.json` is the repository owner's standing configuration and is **out of scope** (otherwise the all-1 smoke walk would break). Switching back to guide is not checked, and resume keeps the record. The record only proves "a sentence was registered", not that the user said it — never claim it as identity proof, and it never enters `agent.summary`.
rules.basis: user decision 2026-11-01 (E2 ruling: the closing check covers runtime goal only; a static default does not block)

rules.text: Know the two layers: the **coordinator** (intake → coordinate → review → done) only dispatches, accepts proposals serially, passes the gates and closes with the final review — it never carries development itself; the **requirement pipeline** has one row per requirement (5 stored states: draft → planning → developing → done, with `analyzing` kept only as a compatibility state; approving the plan gate sets `plan_ok`, the former `ready`, and split / merged / dropped are bypass terminals; display names still distinguish analysis_review / plan_review / plan_gate / ready / dev_review / accept, plus the blocked / stale markers). Dispatch merges analysis into plan: `draft --dispatch--> planning` stores `planning` in the same dispatch.

The two mandatory main-agent gates cannot be skipped: the **plan gate** after a plan proposal is accepted (`req.gate=plan`, only approval sets `plan_ok` and opens development), and the **accept gate** after delivery (`req.gate=accept`, only approval leads to done). While a gate is pending the requirement cannot be dispatched, accepts no new proposal and cannot be skipped, and automatic advancement still runs one `gate.approve` per gate.
A gate is bound to a revision: only `gate_rev == req.rev` may be approved; amending the requirement while the gate is pending makes it stale, and an old approval must never override a newer decision.

`accept` means the **executor self-checked and delivered**; it does not mean the main agent verified — only `gate.approve` does. The accept gate requires **non-empty `artifacts`**; a summary-only completion claim is not accepted.

Actions are dispatched as events whose payload is a pipe-separated string; `settlement.evolution` uses `artifact|summary[|c=<kept>/<screened>[|cls=<kind>:<n>,...]][|sessions=<moved>/<remaining>/<destination>][|todo=<remaining>/<verified_by>]`, and `review.note` uses only `lesson|score`. The `pendingChoice` in a receipt **is the currently allowed action set** (a protocol constraint, not prompt wording) — choose only from it and never invent an action.

Every advancing step is judged by **you (the agent)**, never handed to a script and never defaulted to "always pick the first item": `pendingChoice` is the allowed action set, not a queue to execute — an acceptance that should be rejected must be rejected, a gate that should wait must wait. By design the first item is the main forward action, but it is not guaranteed to be correct at that step.
rules.basis: the decision belongs to the agent, not to a script

rules.text: A refused dispatch is not a success: out of stage → `[REJECTED:ACTION]`, invalid payload → `[REJECTED:PAYLOAD]`, unmet precondition → `[BLOCKED:TODO]`, and a human action dispatched single-shot → `[REJECTED:ACTION]` again. All four re-render in place with the primary state unchanged, and the host reads the narrative prefix to decide "no effect".

The executor only **suggests**: the `changes` of a `proposal.submit` (split / merge / amend / conflict) are proposed changes that land only at `proposal.accept`; an executor may never mutate shared state directly.

Acceptance handles exactly one requirement at a time (serially, in requirement-id canonical order); several requirements may be in analysis / planning / development at once, but acceptance is never parallel.

At acceptance a revision mismatch marks both the proposal and the requirement stale (a readable refusal); the recovery path is a new proposal for the **same stage at the current rev** — accepted only when the requirement has no other pending proposal, otherwise accept / reject the pending one first.

Another process may deliver requirements and proposals at any time through the **inbox** (JSONL, append-only); writes and the closeout are protected by protocol-level mutual exclusion (a writer registers first, the closeout switches to closing, waits for in-flight writers to reach zero, runs one last drain and then becomes finalized). A write command during closing / finalized is refused with a non-zero exit and must never be retried to bypass it.

Inbox consumption is idempotent through `external_id` (replays carry the replay narrative prefix); the cursor only advances after a successful dispatch plus a saved snapshot, so a crash replay never takes effect twice.
An undeclared kind is a malformed line: skip it and advance the cursor (otherwise the queue blocks forever); never retry silently and never roll the whole batch back.

`settle`'s `ok` = the event log is non-empty ∧ no failed step ∧ an ending narrative line appeared ∧ the inbox has no unconsumed line; the exit code mirrors `ok`. Delivering after the ending never silently succeeds — it needs a new run, so the inbox must be drained before closing.

Use the read-only views to inspect progress (requirement graph / two-layer map / field rules) instead of inferring the stage from memory; read the current receipt's `pendingChoice` before dispatching or accepting.

Each run's artifacts live in its run directory (automatic save / event log / run metadata / settlement report / inbox and its cursor / cross-process coordination files); the automatic save can be fed to `load` directly, and the event log holds one line per dispatch. Run directories and executables are never committed.

The pack manifest is **content-addressed** (sha256 + byteLength): editing `data/` or `schemas/` without recomputing the pack makes loading fail with a content-hash mismatch — that is a refusal, not a warning.

In a multi-file Mod the KV prefixes are partitioned by ownership and each prefix has exactly one writer: the kernel / stdlib prefix (`fsm.*`) is written only by `ygg.fsm` and read-only for the Mod, the config-override prefix (`settings.*`) is written only by the config write action, and every other business prefix is owned by its own module. Two modules writing one prefix is implicit coupling — share through a module's return value. This is a documentation convention; loading performs no prefix validation.

Never "glue a multi-file Mod back into one file and then report errors": a module chunk name must carry the real file and line number, a refusal the loader decides itself must carry the call site (`file:line: reason`) and the require chain, and static checks must parse each module independently (a module's `local` never spans chunks). A diagnostic whose line number does not match the real file is a defect.

A multi-file Mod's module chunk performs pure exports only (function and constant definitions) and nothing with side effects: registration / state writes / output all live in the entry. A module exposes registration as a function (`function M.install(deps)`) that the entry calls explicitly in order; touching `ygg.on` / `ygg.emit` / `ygg.narrate` / `ygg.choice` / `ygg.meta` / `ygg.kv.set` / the write members of `ygg.entity` / `ygg.fsm.define` / `ygg.narrative.node` / `ygg.narrative["goto"]` at a module's top level is refused (the static check and the runtime shadow table share one list); at the top level only pure reads are allowed (`ygg.data` / `ygg.ticks` / `ygg.kv.get` / the read members of `ygg.entity`); the entry chunk is exempt (it is the assembly manifest). Why: a handler's dispatch order equals the `ygg.on` registration order — letting a module register itself means "how the files are split / who is required first" decides runtime behavior, so splitting a file or reordering a `require` would change the dispatch order and refactoring would not preserve behavior. `require` is therefore usable at any time (including lazy-loading a pure library inside a handler), but lazy loading never relaxes the boundary: a lazily loaded module's top level is still pure exports. For the details see the Mod authoring guide, section "multi-file Mod", subsection on the side-effect boundary.

After changing a Mod you must finish the trio: ① recompute the pack manifest ② run the Lua static check (0 errors / 0 warnings) ③ run the smoke walk (it must reach the ending). Missing one means the change is not done.

The host carries no defaults: event names, the summary key, the rejection and replay narrative prefixes, the entry default payload, the inbox routes and settlement criteria, and the automatic-advancement thresholds are all declared by the Mod's `pack.json` and static config; a missing section, a missing field, a wrong type or a non-positive integer **fails loading** (fail closed) instead of guessing intent.

The host reads only the structured summary the Mod reports (the receipt's `meta.<metaKey>`) and no Mod-private KV (requirement / proposal / stage / ending keys); the summary surface is a transient receipt and never enters the save or the state hash.
Single-shot mode loads resources from disk in every new process, so a resource change does not need a run restart; a receipt whose source says resume proves the change is in effect.

sections.title: 6. How to propose an evolution (candidate screening · review · scenario first)
sections.summary: An end-of-run suggestion passes four gates before it may enter the backlog: long-term priority, a root cause for an unused existing capability, an independent review per item, and scenario before technique; after verify is green, `settlement.evolution` registers the summary and the candidate declaration, and `review.note` only archives it single-source — the state machine checks the declaration's shape, never the quality of the suggestion.
sections.source: seed template (generic meta-workflow discipline, independent of any repository)

rules.text: A suggestion entering the backlog must by default be a process mechanism that recurs across tasks: the criteria are "would this come up again with another requirement / another repository?" plus "which action of the next run would it change?". Execution constraints of a single task, conventions of a temporary tool or a one-off probe, and anything already solved in that same task do not enter by default.

Every candidate must be classified into exactly one of six classes and counted: `long_term` (long-term mechanism) / `unused` (existing but unused) / `one_off` (single-task constraint) / `temp_tool` (temporary tool) / `redundant` (redundant, to retire) / `no_scene` (genuinely no scenario). Only long_term, unused and redundant may enter the backlog; the other three are recorded as "not adopted" with a stated reason.

"An existing capability is never called" may neither be removed outright nor treated as a missing capability: it must be assigned one of six root causes with locating evidence — the call chain is missing or the entry is unreachable / discoverability is poor / the call cost or contract does not fit / the executor knows about it but chooses not to use it / there genuinely is no scenario / the capability is redundant and should be retired.

Every screened candidate (kept or not) leaves a conclusion in the review artifact with four elements: ① the file and line number; ② a command that can be run as written plus its actual output (not "it was generated"); ③ the semantic basis (does that behavior match or violate the current contract); ④ the root-cause class and the review conclusion (confirmed / insufficient evidence / does not hold / one-off / deferred).
rules.basis: the three elements of the evidence chapter + user decision 2026-11-01 (E1 §4)

rules.text: The narrative order is fixed: which real problem is being solved → which step of the current process is unsatisfied → the code and reproduction evidence → the root cause → the long-term benefit → the change surface and how it is verified. File paths and technical detail only support it and may never replace the problem statement; the user should never have to ask in order to understand the benefit.

After `verify.submit=true`, register with `settlement.evolution`: `artifact|summary[|c=<kept>/<screened>[|cls=<kind>:<n>,...]][|sessions=<moved>/<remaining>/<destination>][|todo=<remaining>/<verified_by>]`. The summary is required after trimming; the artifact may be empty, but **when `screened > 0` it must be `artifacts/<file>.md` and `cls` is required**; the six class counts sum to `screened` and the kept classes sum to `kept`; **c=0/0 allows an empty artifact**. Missing c/cls fall back in order to `settings.review.evolution.*` and then to 0/0 with no classes. Under guide you may pre-register with `config.set review.evolution.artifact|summary|candidates|classes=<value>` (shape checked per key, cross-field completeness only at `settlement.evolution`), and the menu builds the payload from it; with no pre-registration it uses the neutral summary plus c=0/0. The optional `sessions=` / `todo=` segments settle the two end-of-run cleanups in the same transaction. `review.note` afterwards accepts only `lesson|score` and archives the four settlement keys single-source into `review.evolution.*`.
rules.basis: the settlement.evolution / review.note / config.set contracts (this Mod)

rules.text: Never present a registration as proof: the state machine only checks that the summary is non-empty, the path shape, and that the counts and classes are self-consistent — it cannot read the artifact (the sandbox has no filesystem) and does not know whether the review was really performed by an independent subagent. Any claim such as "the suggestion quality is proven" or "the review independence is proven" is out of bounds.
rules.basis: the sandbox allowlist (no io/os) + the settlement.evolution contract

rules.text: Never add a second registration entry point, an external checker script or a host change for the evolution flow: the only registration action is `settlement.evolution`, and the only allowed carriers remain AGENTS.md and the Mod resources (`src/**` and `data/*.json`). Read-only queries may be used to check a declaration but may never become the carrier of a constraint.

sections.title: 7. External tools (two-layer allowlist)
sections.summary: A tool call is a request, never a side effect: the Mod publishes a pending queue in meta.tool_calls, the host executes, and the result comes back as an ordinary tool.result event.
sections.source: the agent-seed host contract (`pack.json` tools + `data/config.json` allowedTools)

rules.text: The Mod never performs IO: no process, no network, no filesystem. It only publishes requests (`meta.tool_calls`) and applies results (`tool.result`).
rules.basis: the sandbox allowlist (no io/os/print) + `ygg.data` is a read-only surface

rules.text: A tool id that is not listed in `data/config.json` `allowedTools` is refused before any row is stored; a missing section allows nothing, and the refusal happens before the id shape is even judged.

A `tool.result` carrying an `external_id` that was already applied is a replay: narrate `[REPLAY:TOOL]`, change no state and never subtract the pending count twice. A different terminal status for the same call is a conflict, not an overwrite.
The tools receipt effect may only latch `tool.notified.<call_id>` and narrate one line; it must never render, choose, or touch requirement / proposal / gate / lane / stage state.

Never inline a credential in a tool declaration or a request: `$ENV{VAR}` placeholders are resolved host-side from the process environment, `<mod_dir>/.env.local` and `<mod_dir>/.env`, and the resolved value never enters a payload, a receipt or a notice — error text names the variable only.
rules.basis: the credentials red line + the host `$ENV{}` resolution order
